title: Food Delivery App System Design: Zomato/Swiggy Case Study
summary: An end-to-end system design of a Zomato/Swiggy-style food delivery app, covering scope, scale estimates, architecture, and each core subsystem: catalog, search, cart, orders, payments, dispatch, tracking, notifications and ETA. It closes with scaling, failure handling, trade-offs and interview questions.

chapters.title: System Design: Food Delivery App (Zomato/Swiggy)
points: Case study: design a three-sided marketplace of customers, restaurants and delivery partners
Scale target: 50M monthly users, 5M orders/day, about 500 orders/s at peak
Subsystems covered: catalog, search, cart, orders, payments, dispatch, tracking, notifications, ETA
Each subsystem chapter follows one template: responsibilities, design, flow, data model, APIs, failures, metrics
Closing chapter covers scaling, failure handling, trade-offs and interview questions

chapters.title: Problem Statement and Scope (Food Delivery App)
points: Problem: a customer orders from a nearby restaurant and a rider delivers it in about 30-40 minutes
Three actors: customer app, restaurant tablet/POS, delivery partner app
Marketplace model (Zomato/Swiggy) vs inventory-led model (cloud kitchens): who owns the food and the fleet
In scope: browse and search, cart, order, pay, dispatch, live tracking, notifications, refunds
Out of scope for this design: restaurant onboarding KYC, rider payouts, ads, loyalty programs
Core user journey in 8 steps: open app, search, view menu, add to cart, pay, restaurant accepts, rider picks up, delivery
Hyperlocal constraint: supply and demand are matched inside a 5-8 km radius, so the system is sharded by city and zone
Time-critical nature: every extra minute of delay raises cancellation rates, so latency is a product metric
Success metrics: order success rate above 99%, delivery time P50 under 32 min, rider utilization above 70%

chapters.title: Requirements and Scale Estimates (Food Delivery App)
points: Functional: search restaurants, view menu, cart, place order, pay, track, rate, cancel and refund
Functional: restaurant accepts or rejects orders and updates menu and stock; rider accepts jobs and updates status
Non-functional: availability 99.95% for ordering, with browse allowed to degrade gracefully
Non-functional: search P99 under 300 ms, order placement P99 under 1 s, tracking update lag under 5 s
Consistency: strong for orders and payments, eventual for search index, ratings and ETAs
Traffic estimate: 5M orders/day, 70% in 4 peak hours, so about 250 orders/s average and about 500/s peak
Browse-to-order ratio of 50:1 gives about 25k read QPS on discovery at peak
Rider location pings: 500k online riders x 1 ping per 5 s = 100k writes/s
Ping storage: 100 B x 100k/s = about 10 MB/s, so about 860 GB/day, kept hot for 7 days then archived
Order storage: 5M orders/day x 2 KB = 10 GB/day, about 3.6 TB/year before replication
Read:write ratio of about 100:1 on catalog, so cache and search replicas dominate the design
Capacity planning: provision for 3x peak on festival days (New Year's Eve, IPL final)

chapters.title: High-Level Architecture (Food Delivery App)
points: Entry path: CDN, then API gateway (auth, rate limiting, routing), then backend-for-frontend per client
Core microservices: catalog, search, cart, order, payment, dispatch, tracking, notification, ETA, pricing
Sync calls (gRPC/REST) for the checkout path; async events on Kafka for everything downstream
Event backbone: Kafka topics order.events, payment.events, rider.location, with a partition key of orderId or riderId
Data stores by workload: PostgreSQL/MySQL for orders, Redis for carts and sessions, Elasticsearch for search, Cassandra or DynamoDB for location history
Geo partitioning: shard by city, then by geohash cell, so a dispatch query never crosses regions
Database-per-service rule: services share data through APIs and events, never through shared tables
Why microservices here: order, tracking and search scale at very different rates, and a team can own each one
Monolith vs microservices: a monolith is simpler to start, but one slow search query can starve checkout
Edge protections: rate limiting at about 10 req/s per user, bot filtering, and idempotency keys on write APIs
Mistake: synchronous chains of 6+ services in checkout; one slow hop multiplies tail latency
Mistake: using one shared database for all services, which creates coupling and a single point of failure

chapters.title: Restaurant Menu and Catalog Service (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: store restaurants, menus, items, prices, availability and operating hours
Scale: about 300k restaurants x 100 items = 30M items, and menu size is about 50 KB per restaurant
Design: write path through a restaurant dashboard or POS integration, read path through a Redis cache with a CDN for images
Flow: restaurant edits an item, catalog DB commit, CDC to Kafka, cache invalidation, search reindex
Data model: Restaurant(id, geo, cuisine, status), MenuItem(id, restaurantId, price, veg, available), ModifierGroup(id, itemId, options)
Price and stock are versioned so a cart can detect that an item changed before checkout
API: GET /restaurants/{id}/menu (cached, P99 under 100 ms) and PATCH /items/{id}/availability
Item-level out-of-stock toggles propagate within 5 s via events, not by polling
Failure: stale cache shows a sold-out item, so the order service re-validates items at checkout
Failure: a POS integration outage means the restaurant is auto-paused after 3 missed heartbeats
Metrics: menu cache hit ratio above 95%, menu staleness P99 under 10 s, item-unavailable rejections per 1k orders

chapters.title: Restaurant Discovery and Search (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: find open, deliverable restaurants and dishes near the user, and rank them well
Search uses Elasticsearch with a geo_point field and filters on cuisine, rating, veg, price and open-now
Serviceability check: only show restaurants whose delivery radius covers the user, usually 5-8 km
Geo indexing options: geohash prefix (precision 5 is about 5 km x 5 km), quadtree, or S2/H3 cells; H3 hexagons give uniform neighbors
Query flow: user location to H3 cell, candidate restaurants from the index, filter by open and serviceable, rank, then fetch menu snippets
Ranking features: distance, ETA, rating, popularity, personal affinity, promos and a restaurant's current kitchen load
Autocomplete uses an edge n-gram or completion suggester with P99 under 100 ms, and typo tolerance of 1-2 edits
Index document holds restaurant and top-dish tokens, and dish-level search needs a separate item index
API: GET /search?q=biryani&lat=..&lng=..&filters=..&cursor=.. with cursor pagination, not offset
Indexing lag: CDC pipeline updates the index in under 10 s; availability flips are applied as partial updates
Failure: if Elasticsearch is down, fall back to a cached list of top restaurants per H3 cell
Metrics: search P99 under 300 ms, zero-result rate under 2%, click-through rate on top 5, index freshness lag

chapters.title: Cart and Checkout (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: hold items, validate prices and stock, apply coupons, compute taxes and fees, then hand off to the order service
One restaurant per cart is a common rule, and adding an item from another restaurant prompts the user to clear the cart
Store: a Redis hash keyed by userId with a 24 h TTL; a DB write happens only when the order is placed
Bill breakdown: item total + GST + delivery fee + packaging + platform fee - discounts = payable
Flow: add item, validate against catalog, reprice, apply coupon, checkout, create a PENDING order, then initiate payment
Cart data model: Cart(userId, restaurantId, items[{itemId, qty, modifiers, priceSnapshot}], couponCode, addressId, version)
Checkout re-validates price, stock, serviceability and restaurant open status; any drift returns a 409 with the new bill
Coupon rules are enforced server-side: per-user limit, minimum order value, expiry and a global budget counter in Redis (atomic DECR)
API: PUT /cart/items, POST /cart/coupon, POST /checkout with an Idempotency-Key header
Failure: a user double-taps pay; the idempotency key makes the second request return the same order
Failure: the coupon budget is exhausted mid-checkout, and the bill is recomputed with a clear message
Metrics: cart-to-order conversion, checkout P99 under 1 s, price-mismatch rate, coupon abuse rate

chapters.title: Order Service and State Machine (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: be the source of truth for the order lifecycle, and orchestrate payment, restaurant, dispatch and notifications
State machine: CREATED, PAYMENT_PENDING, PLACED, ACCEPTED, PREPARING, READY, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, plus CANCELLED and REFUNDED
Transitions are validated in code, so DELIVERED can never move back to PREPARING; each transition is a conditional update (WHERE status = expected)
Restaurant acceptance timeout of 3 min: if there is no response, auto-reject, cancel and refund
Orchestration vs choreography: a saga orchestrator in the order service coordinates steps, with compensations for refund and rider release
Transactional outbox: write the order and the event in one DB transaction, then a relay publishes to Kafka, so no event is lost
Data model: Order(id, userId, restaurantId, status, version, amount, addressSnapshot), OrderItem(...), OrderEvent(orderId, from, to, ts, actor)
Append-only order events provide an audit trail and make it easy to replay and debug
Sharding: orders are sharded by userId for history and indexed by restaurantId for the restaurant dashboard
API: POST /orders, GET /orders/{id}, POST /orders/{id}/cancel, and internal PATCH /orders/{id}/status
Failure: a duplicate Kafka event is handled with idempotent consumers keyed by (orderId, eventId)
Failure: the service crashes after payment but before PLACED, and a reconciler job scans stuck orders every minute
Metrics: order success rate above 99%, restaurant acceptance rate, cancellation rate, time per state (P50 and P99)

chapters.title: Payments and Refunds (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: collect money via UPI, cards, wallets and COD, and handle refunds and reconciliation
Never store raw card data; use a PCI-compliant gateway (Razorpay or Stripe) with tokenization
Flow: order created, payment intent created, user pays at the gateway, webhook confirms, order moves to PLACED
The webhook is the source of truth; the client redirect is only a hint, so also poll the gateway status for 2 min
Idempotency key per order, so one order never creates two charges; the gateway enforces it again
Payment states: INITIATED, PENDING, SUCCESS, FAILED, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED
Data model: Payment(id, orderId, gateway, gatewayTxnId, amount, status, attempts) and Refund(id, paymentId, reason, amount)
Ledger: double-entry records (customer, platform, restaurant, rider) written append-only and never updated
Gateway failover: route UPI traffic to a secondary PSP when the primary success rate falls below 95%
API: POST /payments, POST /webhooks/gateway (signature-verified, idempotent), POST /refunds
Failure: money is debited but the webhook is lost, so a reconciliation job against gateway reports fixes it within 15 min
Failure: a payment succeeds after the order timed out, which triggers an auto-refund
Metrics: payment success rate above 97%, P99 webhook delay, refund turnaround, reconciliation mismatch count

chapters.title: Delivery Partner Assignment (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: pick the best rider for each order, balancing speed, cost and fairness
Rider live locations are kept in a Redis geo index or H3 cells, updated every 5 s
Candidate search: riders within 3 km of the restaurant, available or finishing a drop, sorted by distance
Scoring: pickup ETA, restaurant prep time, rider rating, acceptance rate, current load and direction of travel
Dispatch timing: start assignment when the kitchen is about 8 min from ready, so the rider arrives as food is ready
Batching: one rider can carry 2 orders from nearby restaurants to nearby customers, solved as a bounded assignment problem
Greedy per-order matching vs batch matching every 10-30 s with the Hungarian algorithm: batch gives a better global optimum at the cost of waiting
Offer flow: send the offer to the top rider with a 15 s timeout; on reject or timeout, go to the next candidate
Data model: Rider(id, status, location, activeOrders[]), Assignment(orderId, riderId, status, offeredAt, acceptedAt)
API: POST /dispatch/assign (internal), POST /riders/{id}/offers/{offerId}/accept, PUT /riders/{id}/status
Failure: no riders are available, so the search radius expands in steps and the system adds an incentive or shows a longer ETA
Failure: a rider goes offline after accepting; heartbeat loss of 60 s triggers reassignment
Metrics: assignment time P50 under 20 s, rider acceptance rate, rider idle time, orders per rider per hour

chapters.title: Real-Time Order Tracking (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: ingest rider location pings and show the live map to the customer with a smooth ETA
Ingest path: rider app, then a gateway over MQTT or gRPC, then Kafka (partitioned by riderId), then a location service, then Redis
Load: 100k pings/s at peak, and each ping is about 100 B: (riderId, lat, lng, speed, ts, battery)
Adaptive ping rate: 5 s while moving and 30 s while idle; this saves battery and cuts traffic by about 40%
Push to customer via WebSocket or SSE with updates every 3-5 s; fall back to long polling on poor networks
Subscription model: a WebSocket connection is mapped to orderId, and a pub/sub channel per order fans out each rider update
WebSocket vs polling vs SSE: WebSocket is bidirectional, SSE is simpler and one-way, and polling costs more but is robust
Hot store holds only the latest position per rider (Redis); history goes to Cassandra, TTL 7 days, then S3
Map matching snaps GPS to roads and smooths jitter with a Kalman filter before display
API: WS /track?orderId=.., GET /orders/{id}/location (fallback), POST /riders/location (batched pings)
Failure: a rider loses network, so the app buffers pings and uploads a batch on reconnect, with the server ordering by timestamp
Failure: a WebSocket node dies, and clients reconnect with backoff and jitter to another node
Metrics: location end-to-end lag P99 under 5 s, active WebSocket connections, dropped ping rate, map-match accuracy

chapters.title: Notifications and Communication (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: tell the customer, restaurant and rider about key events, across push, SMS, email and in-app
Channels: push via FCM/APNs (cheap), SMS (costly, used as fallback and for OTP), WhatsApp, and voice calls to restaurants
Event-driven: the notification service consumes order.events and maps each event type to a template and a recipient list
Volume: about 8 notifications per order x 5M orders = 40M/day, about 460/s average and about 2k/s at peak
Pipeline: Kafka, then a preference and dedupe check, then template rendering, then a channel queue, then a provider worker
Priority queues: OTP and 'order accepted' are high priority; promos are low priority and rate-capped per user
Retries use exponential backoff with a dead-letter queue; push failures fall back to SMS for critical messages
Dedupe key (orderId, eventType) prevents a customer getting 'delivered' twice after a replayed event
Data model: Notification(id, userId, type, channel, status, payload, sentAt) and UserPreference(userId, channel, optIn, quietHours)
API: POST /notify (internal), GET /users/{id}/notifications, and a provider delivery-receipt webhook
Failure: a provider outage triggers a circuit breaker and a switch to a backup SMS vendor
Metrics: delivery rate by channel, send latency P99 under 3 s for critical messages, opt-out rate, cost per order

chapters.title: ETA Prediction and Dynamic Pricing (Food Delivery App)
points: Responsibilities: promise an accurate delivery time and balance supply and demand with delivery fees
ETA = restaurant prep time + rider pickup travel + wait + drop travel, each component estimated separately
Prep time is learned per restaurant, per hour and per item count from past orders (gradient boosted trees)
Travel time comes from a road graph plus live traffic, with historical speed profiles by hour
Features: distance, weather, kitchen load, rider supply in the zone, day of week and festival flags
The ETA is shown at browse, cart and tracking; it is recomputed on each state change and every 60 s while in transit
Surge pricing: a zone multiplier from the demand to supply ratio over the last 5 min, capped at about 2x
Fairness guard: show the fee before payment, and lock the quoted fee on the cart so it cannot change at checkout
Data model: EtaPrediction(orderId, predictedAt, estimate, actual) is logged for model feedback
API: GET /eta?restaurantId=&addressId= (P99 under 80 ms) and GET /pricing/zone/{h3}
Failure: when the model service is down, fall back to a rule-based ETA of a static prep time + distance/20 kmph
Metrics: ETA error MAPE under 15%, share of orders late by over 10 min, surge-zone coverage, fee-driven drop-off rate

chapters.title: Scaling, Failure Handling, Trade-offs and Interview Questions (Food Delivery App)
points: Scale horizontally by city: each city is a cell with its own databases and Kafka, and a cell failure affects one city only
Peak handling: pre-scale before lunch and dinner using schedules, and use autoscaling on queue lag and CPU for surges
Caching layers: CDN for images, Redis for menus (TTL 60 s) and carts, and a local in-process cache for config
Load shedding at overload: pause promos and recommendations first, keep search, then checkout, and protect order placement last
Resilience patterns: timeouts of 200-500 ms, retries with jitter and budgets, circuit breakers and bulkheads per dependency
Graceful degradation: serve a stale menu if catalog is down, show a static ETA if the model is down, and fall back from push to SMS
Multi-AZ replicas with automatic failover for databases; RPO near 0 for orders and RTO under 5 min
Consistency trade-off: strong for orders and payments (CP), eventual for search, ratings and live maps (AP)
Sync vs async trade-off: sync gives immediate feedback, and async gives decoupling and absorbs spikes
Common mistakes: no idempotency on payments, no timeouts on gateways, a single Kafka partition key causing hot partitions
Interview Q: how do you avoid double-charging? Use an idempotency key, a webhook as source of truth and a reconciliation job
Interview Q: how do you scale location tracking? Use geo partitioning, adaptive ping rates, latest-only hot store and TTL history
Interview Q: how do you handle a restaurant that never accepts? Use a 3 min timeout, auto-cancel and refund via the saga
Cheatsheet: order = saga + outbox; search = H3 + Elasticsearch; tracking = Kafka + Redis + WebSocket; dispatch = batch matching with a 15 s offer timeout
